chunks: Why measure motor/solenoid speed and position. The question: When/why would knowing the speed and/or position of a motor/solenoid be useful?
The voltage you apply to a motor does not set its speed or position. It only sets what the motor tries to do. Load, supply voltage, and temperature all change the result.
Speed and position measurements let you hold a speed, reach a position, switch a brushless motor's windings at the right moment, and detect stalls and wear.
For a solenoid, you learn whether the plunger arrived.
Think of a shower. Setting the tap to one position does not fix the water temperature. If someone flushes a toilet elsewhere, the water changes with no change at the tap.
To keep it right, you test the water with your hand and adjust. That hand is the sensor, and your adjusting is the feedback.
With a fixed 6. 28 volts the speed falls linearly with load (red).
A speed loop measures the sag and raises the PWM duty to hold 3,000 rpm (blue) until the 12 volts rail is exhausted at about 0. 114 N·m.
Beyond that point no controller can help, which is why sizing the motor and supply still matters.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply. It grows with speed.
Open loop / closed loop: driving with no measurement, or measuring the result and correcting. Speed droop: the drop in speed as load torque rises at a fixed voltage.
Commutation: switching current between a brushless motor's windings in step with the rotor position. Stall: the shaft is stopped while the drive pushes current.
Take a 12 volts motor with a 1 ohms winding. Each rad/s of speed (radian per second, about 9. 5 rpm) makes 0. 02 volts of back-EMF, and each amp makes 0. 02 N·m.
With no load it spins at 12 over 0. 02 equals 600 rad/s, about 5730 rpm. Add a 0. 1 N·m load and it needs 5 amps.
That drops 5 volts across the winding, leaving 7 volts for back-EMF, so speed falls to 350 rad/s, about 3340 rpm. The voltage did not change.
If the shaft stops entirely, the current is 12 over 1 equals 12 amps. That is the whole idea: open-loop speed wanders, so you feed the measurement back.
"Voltage only sets what a motor tries to do.

Load, supply and temperature change what it actually does, so for speed control, positioning, BLDC commutation, stall and jam detection and diagnostics you need to measure speed or position and close the loop.
For a solenoid the equivalent is knowing the plunger arrived, how hard it hit, and whether it jammed, so you can drop to a hold current, soften the landing and flag faults."
Quick check. A brushed DC motor is driven with a fixed PWM duty. Its load torque doubles. What happens to the steady-state speed?
